'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Buried Individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

== Related Literature == {{small|(Literature not used in article writing)}} * {{Cite book|Japanese|editor=Kyoto City|author=|year=1983|chapter=Kofun Period > Ukyo Ward|title=Historical Materials of Kyoto Vol. 2 Archaeology|publisher=[[Heibonsha]]|isbn=|ref={{Harvid|Historical Materials of Kyoto Vol. 2 Archaeology|1983}}}} * {{Cite journal|Japanese|author=Okumura Seiichiro|title=Keyhole-shaped Kofuns in Sagano|date=1993|journal=Kyoto Archaeology|publisher=Kyoto Archaeology Publication Association|volume=|number=72|pages=1-6|url=|naid=|doi=|ref=}} == See Also == {{Commonscat|Tarumiyama Kofun}} * {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Buried Individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Buried Individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Buried Individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|12=draft}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|12=draft}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|12=draft}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|12=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|12=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|12=draft}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|12=draft}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|12=draft}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|12=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|12=draft}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|12=draft}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|12=draft}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|12=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|12=draft}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|12=draft}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|12=draft}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|12=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|12=draft}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|12=draft}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|12=draft}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|12=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.

== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. '''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|12=draft}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
