It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.

Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|12=draft}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|12=draft}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|12=draft}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|12=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|12=draft}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|12=draft}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|12=draft}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|12=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|12=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|12=draft}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|12=draft}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|12=draft}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|12=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|12=draft}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|12=draft}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|12=draft}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|12=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|12=draft}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|12=draft}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|12=draft}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|12=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|12=draft}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|12=draft}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|12=draft}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|12=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|12=draft}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft|12=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|12=draft|12=draft}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|12=draft|12=draft}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|12=draft|12=draft}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=draft|12=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft|12=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft|12=draft}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|12=draft|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|12=draft|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft|12=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft|12=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|12=draft|12=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=draft|12=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft|12=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft|12=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|1=Zenpokoenfun|12=draft|12=draft}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|12=draft|12=draft}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|12=draft|12=draft}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=draft|12=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft|12=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft|12=draft}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|12=draft|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|12=draft|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft|12=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft|12=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|12=draft|12=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=draft|12=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft|12=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=draft|12=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft|12=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft|12=draft}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|12=draft|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|12=draft|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft|12=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft|12=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|12=draft|12=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=draft|12=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft|12=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft|12=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|1=Zenpokoenfun|12=draft|12=draft}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|12=draft|12=draft}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|12=draft|12=draft}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=draft|12=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft|12=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft|12=draft}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|12=draft|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|12=draft|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft|12=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.

[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.

Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.

According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft|12=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|12=draft|12=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=draft|12=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. '''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|12=draft|12=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|1=Zenpokoenfun|12=draft|12=draft}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|12=draft|12=draft}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|12=draft|12=draft}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=draft|12=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=draft|12=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft|12=draft}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|12=draft|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|12=draft|12=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft|12=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|12=draft|12=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=draft|12=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|12=draft|12=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|12=draft|12=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=draft|12=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|12=draft|12=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|qq=draft|qq=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|1=Zenpokoenfun|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.

Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|qq=draft|qq=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

{| class="wikitable" style="background:#ffffff;text-align:center;font-size:85%;" |+太秦・嵯峨野地域の主な古墳{{Sfn|広瀬和雄|2013}} !期!!古墳名!!形状!!規模!!石室全長!!築造時期!!陵墓・史跡 |- | ||'''垂箕山古墳'''||[[前方後円墳]]||65m|| ||5c末-6c初頭||[[宮内庁]]治定墓 |- |rowspan=2|3||rowspan=2|[[天塚古墳]]||rowspan=2|前方後円墳||rowspan=2|73m||(8.1m)||rowspan=2|6c前半||rowspan=2|国の[[史跡]] |- |(7.7m) |- |rowspan=4|4
・
5||[[清水山古墳]]||前方後円墳||57m|| ||rowspan=2|6c中葉-後半||（消滅） |- |段ノ山古墳||前方後円墳|| || ||（消滅） |- |[[双ヶ岡1号墳]]||[[円墳]]||44m||15.8m||rowspan=2|6世紀後半||なし |- |衣笠山1号墳||円墳||26m||(6.0m)||なし |- |rowspan=6|6||[[蛇塚古墳]]||前方後円墳||75m||17.8m||rowspan=6|6c末-7c初頭||国の史跡 |- |[[円山古墳 (京都市)|円山古墳

[[京都盆地]]西部、[[桂川 (淀川水系)|桂川]]左岸の嵯峨野台地に築造された古墳である。現在までに墳丘を良好に遺存する{{Sfn|仲野親王陵（平凡社）|1979}}。現在は[[宮内庁]]治定の[[仲野親王]]墓として同庁の管理下にあり、これまでに本格的な調査はなされていない。 墳形は前方後円形で、前方部を東方に向ける。墳丘長は約63メートル{{Sfn|垂箕山古墳（続古墳）|2002}}（または約75メートル）を測る。特に前方部が極端に広がる形状をとる点が指摘される。また墳丘くびれ部の南側にのみ[[造出]]を有するほか、墳丘周囲には周濠が巡らされる{{Sfn|垂箕山古墳（続古墳）|2002}}。埋葬施設は詳らかでないが、[[明治]]初期の『御陵墓所在書』には[[横穴式石室]]の天井石が描かれることが知られる{{Sfn|垂箕山古墳（続古墳）|2002}}。 築造時期は、[[古墳時代]]後期の[[6世紀]]代（6世紀初頭{{Sfn|垂箕山古墳（続古墳）|2002}}または6世紀中頃{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf 「太秦の古墳を歩く」]}}（京都市埋蔵文化財研究所・京都市考古資料館、2004年）。）と推定される。被葬者は明らかでないが、前述のように現在は宮内庁により[[仲野親王]]（[[貞観 (日本)|貞観]]9年（[[867年]]）死去）の墓に治定されている。嵯峨野地域では、垂箕山古墳のほかにも[[蛇塚古墳]]（墳丘長約75メートル、国の[[史跡]]）・[[天塚古墳]]（墳丘長約71メートル、国の史跡）・清水山古墳（墳丘長約60メートル、非現存）などの後期古墳の分布が知られ、これらは嵯峨野一帯を開発した渡来系氏族の[[秦氏]]一族の墓と推測されており、垂箕山古墳はその中でも古い時期に位置づけられる{{Sfn|広瀬和雄|2013}}。 == 遺跡歴 == * [[1875年]]（[[明治]]8年）、宮内省（現・[[宮内庁]]）により[[仲野親王]]墓に治定{{Sfn|高畠墓（国史）}}。 * [[1989年]]度（[[平成]]元年度）、公共下水道工事に伴う古墳周辺の立会調査（京都市埋蔵文化財研究所、[[1994年]]に報告）{{Sfn|京都市埋蔵文化財調査概要 平成元年度|1994}}。 == 墳丘 == 墳丘の規模は次の通り{{Sfn|垂箕山古墳（続古墳）|2002}}。 * 墳丘長：約63メートル * 後円部 ** 直径：約39メートル ** 高さ：約5メートル * 前方部 ** 幅：約55メートル ** 高さ：約5メートル 1989年度（平成元年度）の古墳周辺における立会調査では、後円部先端で溝が検出されており、丘陵から切り離した際の掘り切り跡と推測される{{Sfn|京都市埋蔵文化財調査概要 平成元年度|1994}}。 == 被葬者 == 垂箕山古墳の実際の被葬者は明らかでないが、[[宮内庁]]では第50代[[桓武天皇]][[皇子]]の'''[[仲野親王]]'''の墓に治定している宮内省諸陵寮編[{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} 『陵墓要覧』]（1934年、国立国会図書館デジタルコレクション）14コマ。{{Sfn|高畠墓（国史）}}『陵墓地形図集成 縮小版』 宮内庁書陵部陵墓課編、学生社、2014年、p. 409。。史書では、仲野親王は[[貞観 (日本)|貞観]]9年（[[867年]]）に没し、[[宇多天皇]]（第59代）の外祖父にあたることから、宇多天皇即位の際には「一品太政大臣」が親王に追贈されたと見える{{Sfn|高畠墓（国史）}}。また『[[延喜式]]』[[諸陵式|諸陵寮]]では、仲野親王の墓は[[山城国]][[葛野郡]]に所在する近墓の「高畠墓」として記載され、墓戸1烟を毎年あてるとする{{Sfn|高畠墓（国史）}}。なお『延喜式』中務省や『[[拾芥抄]]』等では「葛野墓」とも見える{{Sfn|高畠墓（国史）}}。 後世には墓の所在に関する所伝は失われたが、[[1875年]]（[[明治]]8年）に現在の垂箕山古墳が仲野親王墓に治定された{{Sfn|高畠墓（国史）}}。ただし前述のように、垂箕山古墳の築造年代は仲野親王から大きく遡る6世紀中頃と想定され、考古学的には秦氏一族の墓と推測される。一方、この異同については、後世に廃墳状態の垂箕山古墳を利用して仲野親王墓が設置されたと推測する説もある{{Sfn|高畠墓（国史）}}。 [[京都盆地]]西部、[[桂川 (淀川水系)|桂川]]左岸の嵯峨野台地に築造された古墳である。現在までに墳丘を良好に遺存する{{Sfn|仲野親王陵（平凡社）|1979}}。現在は[[宮内庁]]治定の[[仲野親王]]墓として同庁の管理下にあり、これまでに本格的な調査はなされていない。 墳形は前方後円形で、前方部を東方に向ける。墳丘長は約63メートル{{Sfn|垂箕山古墳（続古墳）|2002}}（または約75メートル）を測る。特に前方部が極端に広がる形状をとる点が指摘される。また墳丘くびれ部の南側にのみ[[造出]]を有するほか、墳丘周囲には周濠が巡らされる{{Sfn|垂箕山古墳（続古墳）|2002}}。埋葬施設は詳らかでないが、[[明治]]初期の『御陵墓所在書』には[[横穴式石室]]の天井石が描かれることが知られる{{Sfn|垂箕山古墳（続古墳）|2002}}。 築造時期は、[[古墳時代]]後期の[[6世紀]]代（6世紀初頭{{Sfn|垂箕山古墳（続古墳）|2002}}または6世紀中頃{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf 「太秦の古墳を歩く」]}}（京都市埋蔵文化財研究所・京都市考古資料館、2004年）。）と推定される。被葬者は明らかでないが、前述のように現在は宮内庁により[[仲野親王]]（[[貞観 (日本)|貞観]]9年（[[867年]]）死去）の墓に治定されている。嵯峨野地域では、垂箕山古墳のほかにも[[蛇塚古墳]]（墳丘長約75メートル、国の[[史跡]]）・[[天塚古墳]]（墳丘長約71メートル、国の史跡）・清水山古墳（墳丘長約60メートル、非現存）などの後期古墳の分布が知られ、これらは嵯峨野一帯を開発した渡来系氏族の[[秦氏]]一族の墓と推測されており、垂箕山古墳はその中でも古い時期に位置づけられる{{Sfn|広瀬和雄|2013}}。 == 遺跡歴 == * [[1875年]]（[[明治]]8年）、宮内省（現・[[宮内庁]]）により[[仲野親王]]墓に治定{{Sfn|高畠墓（国史）}}。 * [[1989年]]度（[[平成]]元年度）、公共下水道工事に伴う古墳周辺の立会調査（京都市埋蔵文化財研究所、[[1994年]]に報告）{{Sfn|京都市埋蔵文化財調査概要 平成元年度|1994}}。 == 墳丘 == 墳丘の規模は次の通り{{Sfn|垂箕山古墳（続古墳）|2002}}。 * 墳丘長：約63メートル * 後円部 ** 直径：約39メートル ** 高さ：約5メートル * 前方部 ** 幅：約55メートル ** 高さ：約5メートル 1989年度（平成元年度）の古墳周辺における立会調査では、後円部先端で溝が検出されており、丘陵から切り離した際の掘り切り跡と推測される{{Sfn|京都市埋蔵文化財調査概要 平成元年度|1994}}。 == 被葬者 == 垂箕山古墳の実際の被葬者は明らかでないが、[[宮内庁]]では第50代[[桓武天皇]][[皇子]]の'''[[仲野親王]]'''の墓に治定している宮内省諸陵寮編[{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} 『陵墓要覧』]（1934年、国立国会図書館デジタルコレクション）14コマ。{{Sfn|高畠墓（国史）}}『陵墓地形図集成 縮小版』 宮内庁書陵部陵墓課編、学生社、2014年、p. 409。。史書では、仲野親王は[[貞観 (日本)|貞観]]9年（[[867年]]）に没し、[[宇多天皇]]（第59代）の外祖父にあたることから、宇多天皇即位の際には「一品太政大臣」が親王に追贈されたと見える{{Sfn|高畠墓（国史）}}。また『[[延喜式]]』[[諸陵式|諸陵寮]]では、仲野親王の墓は[[山城国]][[葛野郡]]に所在する近墓の「高畠墓」として記載され、墓戸1烟を毎年あてるとする{{Sfn|高畠墓（国史）}}。なお『延喜式』中務省や『[[拾芥抄]]』等では「葛野墓」とも見える{{Sfn|高畠墓（国史）}}。 後世には墓の所在に関する所伝は失われたが、[[1875年]]（[[明治]]8年）に現在の垂箕山古墳が仲野親王墓に治定された{{Sfn|高畠墓（国史）}}。ただし前述のように、垂箕山古墳の築造年代は仲野親王から大きく遡る6世紀中頃と想定され、考古学的には秦氏一族の墓と推測される。一方、この異同については、後世に廃墳状態の垂箕山古墳を利用して仲野親王墓が設置されたと推測する説もある{{Sfn|高畠墓（国史）}}。
