'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|qq=draft|qq=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|1=Zenpokoenfun|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|qq=draft|qq=draft}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=draft|qq=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|qq=draft|qq=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|qq=draft|qq=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|qq=draft|qq=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|1=Zenpokoenfun|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|qq=draft|qq=draft}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=draft|qq=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|1=Hebizuka Kofun|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|qq=draft|qq=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|qq=draft|qq=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|qq=draft|qq=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|1=Zenpokoenfun|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|qq=draft|qq=draft}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=draft|qq=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|1=Hebizuka Kofun|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|qq=draft|qq=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|qq=draft|qq=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|qq=draft|qq=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|qq=draft|qq=draft}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|1=Zenpokoenfun|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|qq=draft|qq=draft}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=draft|qq=draft}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|1=Hebizuka Kofun|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|qq=draft|qq=draft}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|qq=draft|qq=draft}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Kofun|qq=}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|1=Zenpokoenfun|1=Zenpokoenfun|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/keyhole-shaped Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Zenpokoenfun|qq=}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Household Agency|qq=}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto Basin|qq=}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Katsura River|qq=}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Household Agency|qq=}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukuridashi|13=User:Immanuelle/Platform-style projection|qq=}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/corridor-style stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Household Agency|qq=}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jogan era|qq=}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|1=Hebizuka Kofun|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hebizuka Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Hebizuka Kofun|qq=}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amatsuka Kofun|qq=}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hata Clan|qq=}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Household Agency|qq=}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Household Agency|qq=}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jogan era|qq=}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki|qq=}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Katsuno District|qq=}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hata Clan|qq=}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto Basin|qq=}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|ja|桂川 (淀川水系)|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Katsura River|qq=}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Household Agency|qq=}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukuridashi|13=User:Immanuelle/Platform-style projection|qq=}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/corridor-style stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Household Agency|qq=}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jogan era|qq=}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|ja|蛇塚古墳|1=Hebizuka Kofun|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hebizuka Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Hebizuka Kofun|qq=}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|ja|天塚古墳|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amatsuka Kofun|qq=}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hata Clan|qq=}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Household Agency|qq=}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|ja|宮内庁|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Household Agency|qq=}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the {{ill|Jogan era|ja|貞観|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jogan era|qq=}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Engishiki|qq=}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Katsuno District|qq=}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hata Clan|qq=}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|ja|古墳|1=Kofun|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Kofun|qq=}} located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|keyhole-shaped Kofun|ja|前方後円墳|lt=Zenpokoenfun|1=Zenpokoenfun|comment=doing this because I need to differentiate it in piped links too with my new interwiki tool as not the ambiguous phrase keyhole shaped kofun|1=Zenpokoenfun|1=Zenpokoenfun|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/keyhole-shaped Kofun|13=User:Immanuelle/Zenpokoenfun|qq=}}.

However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata Clan|ja|秦氏|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hata Clan|qq=}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a [[:en:Kofun|Kofun]] located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a [[:en:Zenpokoenfun|Zenpokoenfun]].
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto Basin|qq=}} on the left bank of the [[:en:Katsura River|Katsura River]], the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukuridashi|13=User:Immanuelle/Platform-style projection|qq=}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/corridor-style stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} (died in 867 during the [[:en:Zhenguan|Jogan era]]). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include [[:en:Hebizuka Kofun|Hebizuka Kofun]] (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), [[:en:Amatsuka Kofun|Amatsuka Kofun]] (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant [[:en:Hata clan|Hata Clan]] who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]]){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the [[:en:Zhenguan|Jogan era]] and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the [[:en:Engishiki|Engishiki]] "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Katsuno District|qq=}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the [[:en:Hata clan|Hata Clan]]. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a [[:en:Kofun|Kofun]] located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a [[:en:Zenpokoenfun|Zenpokoenfun]].
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto Basin|qq=}} on the left bank of the [[:en:Katsura River|Katsura River]], the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukuridashi|13=User:Immanuelle/Platform-style projection|qq=}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/corridor-style stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} (died in 867 during the [[:en:Zhenguan|Jogan era]]). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include [[:en:Hebizuka Kofun|Hebizuka Kofun]] (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), [[:en:Amatsuka Kofun|Amatsuka Kofun]] (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant [[:en:Hata clan|Hata Clan]] who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]]){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the [[:en:Zhenguan|Jogan era]] and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the [[:en:Engishiki|Engishiki]] "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Katsuno District|qq=}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the [[:en:Hata clan|Hata Clan]]. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a [[:en:Kofun|Kofun]] located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a [[:en:Zenpokoenfun|Zenpokoenfun]].
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto Basin|qq=}} on the left bank of the [[:en:Katsura River|Katsura River]], the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukuridashi|13=User:Immanuelle/Platform-style projection|qq=}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/corridor-style stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} (died in 867 during the [[:en:Zhenguan|Jogan era]]). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include [[:en:Hebizuka Kofun|Hebizuka Kofun]] (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), [[:en:Amatsuka Kofun|Amatsuka Kofun]] (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant [[:en:Hata clan|Hata Clan]] who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]]){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the [[:en:Zhenguan|Jogan era]] and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the [[:en:Engishiki|Engishiki]] "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Katsuno District|qq=}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the [[:en:Hata clan|Hata Clan]]. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a [[:en:Kofun|Kofun]] located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a [[:en:Zenpokoenfun|Zenpokoenfun]].
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto Basin|qq=}} on the left bank of the [[:en:Katsura River|Katsura River]], the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukuridashi|13=User:Immanuelle/Platform-style projection|qq=}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/corridor-style stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} (died in 867 during the [[:en:Zhenguan|Jogan era]]). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include [[:en:Hebizuka Kofun|Hebizuka Kofun]] (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), [[:en:Amatsuka Kofun|Amatsuka Kofun]] (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant [[:en:Hata clan|Hata Clan]] who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]]){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the [[:en:Zhenguan|Jogan era]] and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the [[:en:Engishiki|Engishiki]] "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Katsuno District|qq=}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the [[:en:Hata clan|Hata Clan]]. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a [[:en:Kofun|Kofun]] located in [[Kyoto Prefecture]], [[Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a [[:en:Zenpokoenfun|Zenpokoenfun]].
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto Basin|qq=}} on the left bank of the [[:en:Katsura River|Katsura River]], the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukuridashi|13=User:Immanuelle/Platform-style projection|qq=}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/corridor-style stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the [[6th century]] (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} (died in 867 during the [[:en:Zhenguan|Jogan era]]). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include [[:en:Hebizuka Kofun|Hebizuka Kofun]] (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), [[:en:Amatsuka Kofun|Amatsuka Kofun]] (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant [[:en:Hata clan|Hata Clan]] who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
[[1875]] (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]]){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
[[1989]] (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in [[1994]] by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in [[867]] during the [[:en:Zhenguan|Jogan era]] and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the [[:en:Engishiki|Engishiki]] "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Katsuno District|qq=}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in [[1875]] (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the [[:en:Hata clan|Hata Clan]]. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
