'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|en|Kofun|WD=Q1141225|lt=Kofun|1=Kofun}} located in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|en|Kyoto Prefecture|WD=Q120730|lt=Kyoto Prefecture|1=Kyoto Prefecture}}, [[:en:Kyoto City|Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|Zenpokoenfun|en|Zenpokoenfun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpokoenfun|1=Zenpōkōenfun}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto Basin|1=Kyoto Basin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10883263}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|en|Katsura River|WD=Q2909307|lt=Katsura River|1=Katsura River}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukuridashi|13=User:Immanuelle/Platform-style projection|qq=}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/corridor-style stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the {{ill|6th century|en|6th century|WD=Q8090|lt=6th century|1=6th century}} (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Zhenguan|en|Zhenguan|WD=Q3577278|lt=Jogan era|1=Zhenguan}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|en|Hebizuka Kofun|WD=Q11625508|lt=Hebizuka Kofun|1=Hebizuka Kofun}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|en|Amatsuka Kofun|WD=Q11442478|lt=Amatsuka Kofun|1=Amatsuka Kofun}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata clan|en|Hata clan|WD=Q987290|lt=Hata Clan|1=Hata clan}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
{{ill|1875|en|1875|WD=Q7764|lt=1875|1=1875}} (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
{{ill|1989|en|1989|WD=Q2425|lt=1989|1=1989}} (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in {{ill|1994|en|1994|WD=Q2067|lt=1994|1=1994}} by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in {{ill|867|en|867|WD=Q30347|lt=867|1=867}} during the {{ill|Zhenguan|en|Zhenguan|WD=Q3577278|lt=Jogan era|1=Zhenguan}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|en|Engishiki|WD=Q1342448|lt=Engishiki|1=Engishiki}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Katsuno District|1=Kadono district|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q13579879}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in {{ill|1875|en|1875|WD=Q7764|lt=1875|1=1875}} (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata clan|en|Hata clan|WD=Q987290|lt=Hata Clan|1=Hata clan}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

In the {{ill|Engishiki|en|Engishiki|WD=Q1342448|lt=Engishiki|1=Engishiki}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Katsuno District|1=Kadono district|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q13579879}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in {{ill|1875|en|1875|WD=Q7764|lt=1875|1=1875}} (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata clan|en|Hata clan|WD=Q987290|lt=Hata Clan|1=Hata clan}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|en|Kofun|WD=Q1141225|lt=Kofun|1=Kofun}} located in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|en|Kyoto Prefecture|WD=Q120730|lt=Kyoto Prefecture|1=Kyoto Prefecture}}, [[:en:Kyoto City|Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|Zenpō-kōen-fun|en|Zenpō-kōen-fun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpō-kōen-fun|1=Zenpō-kōen-fun}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto Basin|1=Kyoto Basin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10883263}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|en|Katsura River|WD=Q2909307|lt=Katsura River|1=Katsura River}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukuridashi|13=User:Immanuelle/Platform-style projection|qq=}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/corridor-style stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the {{ill|6th century|en|6th century|WD=Q8090|lt=6th century|1=6th century}} (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Zhenguan|en|Zhenguan|WD=Q3577278|lt=Jogan era|1=Zhenguan}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|en|Hebizuka Kofun|WD=Q11625508|lt=Hebizuka Kofun|1=Hebizuka Kofun}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|en|Amatsuka Kofun|WD=Q11442478|lt=Amatsuka Kofun|1=Amatsuka Kofun}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata clan|en|Hata clan|WD=Q987290|lt=Hata Clan|1=Hata clan}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
{{ill|1875|en|1875|WD=Q7764|lt=1875|1=1875}} (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
{{ill|1989|en|1989|WD=Q2425|lt=1989|1=1989}} (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in {{ill|1994|en|1994|WD=Q2067|lt=1994|1=1994}} by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in {{ill|867|en|867|WD=Q30347|lt=867|1=867}} during the {{ill|Zhenguan|en|Zhenguan|WD=Q3577278|lt=Jogan era|1=Zhenguan}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|en|Engishiki|WD=Q1342448|lt=Engishiki|1=Engishiki}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Katsuno District|1=Kadono district|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q13579879}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in {{ill|1875|en|1875|WD=Q7764|lt=1875|1=1875}} (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata clan|en|Hata clan|WD=Q987290|lt=Hata Clan|1=Hata clan}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

'''Tarumiyama Kofun''' (垂箕山古墳), also known as Katahira Otsuka Kofun{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}, is a {{ill|Kofun|en|Kofun|WD=Q1141225|lt=Kofun|1=Kofun}} located in {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|en|Kyoto Prefecture|WD=Q120730|lt=Kyoto Prefecture|1=Kyoto Prefecture}}, [[:en:Kyoto City|Kyoto City]], [[Ukyo Ward]], Uzumasa Tarumiyama Town. Its type is a {{ill|Zenpō-kōen-fun|en|Zenpō-kōen-fun|WD=Q11268718|lt=Zenpō-kōen-fun|1=Zenpō-kōen-fun}}.
The actual identity of the buried individual is unclear, but the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}} has designated it as "Takabatake Tomb," the burial site of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, son of the 50th emperor, Emperor Kanmu.
== Overview ==
Located in the western {{ill|Kyoto Basin|ja|京都盆地|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyoto Basin|1=Kyoto Basin|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q10883263}} on the left bank of the {{ill|Katsura River|en|Katsura River|WD=Q2909307|lt=Katsura River|1=Katsura River}}, the mound is well-preserved{{Sfn|Nakano Prince's Mausoleum (Heibonsha)|1979}}. It is currently managed by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}} as the designated tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, and no formal archaeological investigations have been conducted to date.
The mound is keyhole-shaped, oriented eastward with a total length of approximately 63 meters{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} (or about 75 meters). Notably, its front rectangular section exhibits an unusually wide type. In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukuridashi|13=User:Immanuelle/Platform-style projection|qq=}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/corridor-style stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the {{ill|6th century|en|6th century|WD=Q8090|lt=6th century|1=6th century}} (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Zhenguan|en|Zhenguan|WD=Q3577278|lt=Jogan era|1=Zhenguan}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|en|Hebizuka Kofun|WD=Q11625508|lt=Hebizuka Kofun|1=Hebizuka Kofun}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|en|Amatsuka Kofun|WD=Q11442478|lt=Amatsuka Kofun|1=Amatsuka Kofun}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata clan|en|Hata clan|WD=Q987290|lt=Hata Clan|1=Hata clan}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
{{ill|1875|en|1875|WD=Q7764|lt=1875|1=1875}} (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
{{ill|1989|en|1989|WD=Q2425|lt=1989|1=1989}} (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in {{ill|1994|en|1994|WD=Q2067|lt=1994|1=1994}} by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in {{ill|867|en|867|WD=Q30347|lt=867|1=867}} during the {{ill|Zhenguan|en|Zhenguan|WD=Q3577278|lt=Jogan era|1=Zhenguan}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|en|Engishiki|WD=Q1342448|lt=Engishiki|1=Engishiki}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Katsuno District|1=Kadono district|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q13579879}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in {{ill|1875|en|1875|WD=Q7764|lt=1875|1=1875}} (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata clan|en|Hata clan|WD=Q987290|lt=Hata Clan|1=Hata clan}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.

In addition, the southern side of the neck area features a {{ill|Tsukuridashi|ja|造出|1=Platform-style projection|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tsukuridashi|13=User:Immanuelle/Platform-style projection|qq=}}, and a moat encircles the mound{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}. Details of the burial facility are unclear, but the early Meiji-period "Onryobo Shozaisho" records depict the ceiling stone of a {{ill|corridor-style stone chamber|ja|横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|2=ja|3=横穴式石室|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|4=zh|5=橫穴式石室|6=ko|7=굴식 돌방무덤|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|1=Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/corridor-style stone chamber|13=User:Immanuelle/Corridor-Style Stone Chamber|qq=}}{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}.
The construction period is estimated to be the late [[Kofun period]], during the {{ill|6th century|en|6th century|WD=Q8090|lt=6th century|1=6th century}} (early 6th century{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}} or mid-6th century{{PDFlink|[http://www.kyoto-arc.or.jp/news/leaflet/190.pdf "Walking Through Uzumasa's Kofun"]}} (Kyoto Archaeological Research Institute & Kyoto City Archaeological Museum, 2004).). While the identity of the buried individual remains uncertain, as mentioned, it is designated by the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}} as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} (died in 867 during the {{ill|Zhenguan|en|Zhenguan|WD=Q3577278|lt=Jogan era|1=Zhenguan}}). In the Sagano area, other late-period kofun include {{ill|Hebizuka Kofun|en|Hebizuka Kofun|WD=Q11625508|lt=Hebizuka Kofun|1=Hebizuka Kofun}} (mound length approx. 75 meters, national historic site), {{ill|Amatsuka Kofun|en|Amatsuka Kofun|WD=Q11442478|lt=Amatsuka Kofun|1=Amatsuka Kofun}} (mound length approx. 71 meters, national historic site), and Shimizuyama Kofun (mound length approx. 60 meters, destroyed), all associated with the immigrant {{ill|Hata clan|en|Hata clan|WD=Q987290|lt=Hata Clan|1=Hata clan}} who developed the Sagano region. Tarumiyama Kofun is considered one of the earlier examples among them{{Sfn|Hirose Kazuo|2013}}.
== History ==
{{ill|1875|en|1875|WD=Q7764|lt=1875|1=1875}} (Meiji 8): Designated as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}} by the Ministry of the Imperial Household (now {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}}){{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
{{ill|1989|en|1989|WD=Q2425|lt=1989|1=1989}} (Heisei 1): Monitoring of the area surrounding the kofun during public sewage construction (reported in {{ill|1994|en|1994|WD=Q2067|lt=1994|1=1994}} by the Kyoto City Archaeological Research Institute){{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Mound Specifications == The map_size of the mound is as follows{{Sfn|Tarumiyama Kofun (Supplement)|2002}}:
Total length: Approx. 63 meters
Rear circular section ''' Diameter: Approx. 39 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
Front rectangular section ''' Width: Approx. 55 meters ''' Height: Approx. 5 meters
A trench was discovered at the rear circular section during the 1989 survey, believed to mark the site where the mound was detached from the surrounding hill{{Sfn|Kyoto City Archaeological Report 1989|1994}}.
== Interred_individual == While the actual identity of the buried individual remains unclear, the {{ill|Imperial Household Agency|en|Imperial Household Agency|WD=Q1143602|lt=Imperial Household Agency|1=Imperial Household Agency}} has designated Tarumiyama Kofun as the tomb of {{ill|Prince Nakano|ja|仲野親王|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Prince Nakano|qq=}}, son of Emperor KanmuCompiled by the Ministry of the Imperial Household, [{{NDLDC|1237123/14}} "Compendium of Mausoleum locations"] (1934, National Diet Library Digital Collections), Frame 14.{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}"Compendium of Mausoleum maps," compiled by the Imperial Household Agency's Archives Section, Student Publishing Co., 2014, p. 409.. According to historical records, Prince Nakano passed away in {{ill|867|en|867|WD=Q30347|lt=867|1=867}} during the {{ill|Zhenguan|en|Zhenguan|WD=Q3577278|lt=Jogan era|1=Zhenguan}} and was posthumously honored with the title of "Senior First Rank Chancellor" when Emperor Uda ascended the throne{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. In the {{ill|Engishiki|en|Engishiki|WD=Q1342448|lt=Engishiki|1=Engishiki}} "Shoryo" chapter, his tomb is recorded as the "Takabatake Tomb" in {{ill|Katsuno District|ja|葛野郡|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Katsuno District|1=Kadono district|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q13579879}}, Yamashiro Province, with an annual allotment of one family to manage the tomb{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. Later records such as the "Engishiki" Ministry of Central Affairs chapter and the "Shukai-sho" refer to it as "Katsuno Tomb"{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
Over time, the location of the tomb became uncertain, but in {{ill|1875|en|1875|WD=Q7764|lt=1875|1=1875}} (Meiji 8), the current Tarumiyama Kofun was designated as the tomb of Prince Nakano{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}. However, as previously mentioned, archaeological evidence suggests the kofun predates Prince Nakano by several centuries, dating back to the mid-6th century, and is more likely associated with the {{ill|Hata clan|en|Hata clan|WD=Q987290|lt=Hata Clan|1=Hata clan}}. An alternative theory posits that the tomb of Prince Nakano was established within the already disused Tarumiyama Kofun{{Sfn|Takabatake Tomb (National History)}}.
